stem: What is the resistance of one of the rails of a railway track 20 km long at \(20^{\circ}\)C? The cross section area of rail is 25 cm\(^{2}\) and the rail is made of steel having resistivity at \(20^{\circ}\)C as \(6 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\) m.
our_solution:
**Data:** length \( L = 20 \) km \( = 20 \times 10^{3} \) m, area of cross section \( A = 25 \) cm\(^{2}\) \( = 25 \times 10^{-4} \) m\(^{2}\), resistivity \( \rho = 6 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\text{m} \) at \( 20^{\circ} \)C.

**Relation:** the resistance of a uniform conductor is \( R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} \).

Note that both the resistivity and the required resistance are quoted at the same temperature \( 20^{\circ} \)C, so no temperature correction is needed.

**Substitution:**

\( R = \dfrac{(6 \times 10^{-8})(20 \times 10^{3})}{25 \times 10^{-4}} \)

\( R = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-3}}{2.5 \times 10^{-3}} \)

\( R = 0.48\ \Omega \)

**Answer: the resistance of one rail is \( R = 0.48\ \Omega \).**

stem: A battery after a long use has an emf 24 V and an internal resistance \(380\ \Omega\). Calculate the maximum current drawn from the battery? Can this battery drive starting motor of car?
our_solution:
**Data:** emf \( \varepsilon = 24 \) V, internal resistance \( r = 380\ \Omega \).

**Relation:** for a cell of emf \( \varepsilon \) and internal resistance \( r \) driving an external resistance \( R \),

\( I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r} \)

This current is largest when the external resistance is made as small as possible, i.e. \( R = 0 \) (terminals directly connected). Hence

\( I_{\max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r} \)

**Substitution:**

\( I_{\max} = \dfrac{24}{380} = 6.316 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A} \approx 63.2 \) mA

**Can it drive the starting motor of a car?** No. The starting (cranking) motor of a car needs a current of the order of \( 100 \) A. The largest current this battery can supply is about \( 0.063 \) A, which is smaller by a factor of roughly \( 10^{3} \). Long use has raised the internal resistance to \( 380\ \Omega \), and because \( r \) appears in the denominator of \( I = \varepsilon /(R+r) \), such a large internal resistance chokes the current no matter how small the external resistance is made. The battery may still show \( 24 \) V on a voltmeter (which draws almost no current), but it cannot deliver useful power.

**Answer: \( I_{\max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r} = 6.32 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A} \approx 63.2 \) mA; no, this battery cannot drive the starting motor of a car.**

stem:
A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance \(3\ \Omega\) is connected to a resistor. If the current in the circuit is 0.5 A,
a] Calculate resistance of resistor.
b] Calculate terminal voltage of the battery when the circuit is closed.
our_solution:
**Data:** emf \( \varepsilon = 12 \) V, internal resistance \( r = 3\ \Omega \), current \( I = 0.5 \) A.

**a] Resistance of the resistor**

For a closed circuit, \( \varepsilon = I(R + r) \), so

\( R + r = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{I} = \dfrac{12}{0.5} = 24\ \Omega \)

\( R = 24 - 3 = 21\ \Omega \)

**b] Terminal voltage with the circuit closed**

The terminal voltage is the emf less the potential drop inside the cell:

\( V = \varepsilon - I r = 12 - (0.5)(3) = 12 - 1.5 = 10.5 \) V

*Cross-check:* the terminal voltage must also equal the potential difference across the external resistor, \( V = I R = (0.5)(21) = 10.5 \) V. The two agree.

**Answer: a] \( R = 21\ \Omega \)  b] \( V = 10.5 \) V.**

stem: The magnitude of current density in a copper wire is 500 A/cm\(^{2}\). If the number of free electrons per cm\(^{3}\) of copper is \(8.47 \times 10^{22}\) calculate the drift velocity of the electrons through the copper wire (charge on an \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C)
our_solution:
**Data:** current density \( J = 500 \) A/cm\(^{2}\), free electron density \( n = 8.47 \times 10^{22} \) per cm\(^{3}\), charge on an electron \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C.

**Relation:** the current density in a conductor is \( J = n e v_{d} \), so the drift speed is

\( v_{d} = \dfrac{J}{n e} \)

The data are given per cm\(^{2}\) and per cm\(^{3}\), so working in those units directly gives \( v_{d} \) in cm/s.

**Substitution:**

\( n e = (8.47 \times 10^{22})(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 1.3552 \times 10^{4}\ \text{C/cm}^{3} \)

\( v_{d} = \dfrac{500}{1.3552 \times 10^{4}} = 3.689 \times 10^{-2} \) cm/s

In SI units, \( v_{d} = 3.689 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{cm/s} = 3.689 \times 10^{-4} \) m/s.

*(Cross-check in SI: \( J = 500\ \text{A/cm}^{2} = 5 \times 10^{6}\ \text{A/m}^{2} \) and \( n = 8.47 \times 10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3} \), giving \( v_{d} = 5 \times 10^{6}/(8.47 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 3.689 \times 10^{-4} \) m/s — the same value.)*

This very small drift speed — a few tenths of a millimetre per second — is characteristic of metallic conduction: the electrons drift slowly, even though the electric signal itself travels almost instantaneously.

**Answer: \( v_{d} = 3.69 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{cm/s} = 3.69 \times 10^{-4} \) m/s.**

stem:
Three resistors \(10\ \Omega\), \(20\ \Omega\) and \(30\ \Omega\) are connected in series combination.
i] Find equivalent resistance of series combination.
ii] When this series combination is connected to 12V supply, by neglecting the value of internal resistance, obtain potential difference across each resistor.
our_solution:
**Data:** \( R_{1} = 10\ \Omega \), \( R_{2} = 20\ \Omega \), \( R_{3} = 30\ \Omega \) in series; supply \( V = 12 \) V; internal resistance neglected.

**i] Equivalent resistance of the series combination**

In series the resistances simply add:

\( R_{s} = R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3} = 10 + 20 + 30 = 60\ \Omega \)

**ii] Potential difference across each resistor**

In a series circuit the same current flows through every resistor:

\( I = \dfrac{V}{R_{s}} = \dfrac{12}{60} = 0.2 \) A

Applying \( V = IR \) to each resistor,

\( V_{1} = I R_{1} = (0.2)(10) = 2 \) V

\( V_{2} = I R_{2} = (0.2)(20) = 4 \) V

\( V_{3} = I R_{3} = (0.2)(30) = 6 \) V

*Cross-check:* \( V_{1} + V_{2} + V_{3} = 2 + 4 + 6 = 12 \) V, which equals the supply voltage as it must.

**Answer: i] \( R_{s} = 60\ \Omega \)  ii] \( V_{1} = 2 \) V across \( 10\ \Omega \), \( V_{2} = 4 \) V across \( 20\ \Omega \), \( V_{3} = 6 \) V across \( 30\ \Omega \) (current \( I = 0.2 \) A).**

stem:
Two resistors \(1\text{k}\ \Omega\) and \(2\text{k}\ \Omega\) are connected in parallel combination.
i] Find equivalent resistance of parallel combination
ii] When this parallel combination is connected to 9 V supply, by neglecting internal resistance calculate current through each resistor.
our_solution:
**Data:** \( R_{1} = 1\ \text{k}\Omega = 1000\ \Omega \), \( R_{2} = 2\ \text{k}\Omega = 2000\ \Omega \) in parallel; supply \( V = 9 \) V; internal resistance neglected.

**i] Equivalent resistance of the parallel combination**

\( \dfrac{1}{R_{p}} = \dfrac{1}{R_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1000} + \dfrac{1}{2000} = \dfrac{3}{2000} \)

\( R_{p} = \dfrac{2000}{3} = 666.7\ \Omega \approx 0.667\ \text{k}\Omega \)

As expected, \( R_{p} \) is smaller than either resistor.

**ii] Current through each resistor**

In parallel the same potential difference, \( 9 \) V, appears across both resistors, so each current follows from \( I = V/R \):

\( I_{1} = \dfrac{9}{1000} = 9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 9 \) mA

\( I_{2} = \dfrac{9}{2000} = 4.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 4.5 \) mA

*Cross-check:* the total current drawn from the supply is \( I_{1} + I_{2} = 13.5 \) mA, and \( V/R_{p} = 9/666.7 = 13.5 \) mA. The two agree.

**Answer: i] \( R_{p} = 666.7\ \Omega \approx 0.67\ \text{k}\Omega \)  ii] \( I_{1} = 9 \) mA through the \( 1\ \text{k}\Omega \), \( I_{2} = 4.5 \) mA through the \( 2\ \text{k}\Omega \).**

stem: A silver wire has a resistance of \(4.2\ \Omega\) at \(27^{\circ}\)C and resistance \(5.4\ \Omega\) at \(100^{\circ}\)C. Determine the temperature coefficient of resistance.
our_solution:
**Data:** \( R_{1} = 4.2\ \Omega \) at \( T_{1} = 27^{\circ} \)C, \( R_{2} = 5.4\ \Omega \) at \( T_{2} = 100^{\circ} \)C.

**Relation:** taking \( R_{1} \) as the reference resistance, the variation of resistance with temperature is

\( R_{2} = R_{1}\left[1 + \alpha (T_{2} - T_{1})\right] \)

\( \therefore\ \alpha = \dfrac{R_{2} - R_{1}}{R_{1}(T_{2} - T_{1})} \)

**Substitution:**

\( R_{2} - R_{1} = 5.4 - 4.2 = 1.2\ \Omega \)

\( T_{2} - T_{1} = 100 - 27 = 73^{\circ} \)C

\( \alpha = \dfrac{1.2}{(4.2)(73)} = \dfrac{1.2}{306.6} \)

\( \alpha = 3.914 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{per}\ ^{\circ}\text{C} \)

Since a Celsius degree and a kelvin are the same size, this may equally be written \( \alpha = 3.914 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{K}^{-1} \). The positive sign confirms that the resistance of silver, a metal, *increases* with temperature.

**Answer: \( \alpha = 3.91 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{per}\ ^{\circ}\text{C} \) (referred to \( 27^{\circ} \)C).**

stem: A 6m long wire has diameter 0.5 mm. Its resistance is \(50\ \Omega\). Find the resistivity and conductivity.
our_solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the units as \(\Omega/\text{m}\) and \(\text{m}/\Omega\). Both VALUES are correct, and both units are not. Resistivity is \(\rho = RA/L\), which carries \(\Omega\,\text{m}\); conductivity is its reciprocal, \((\Omega\,\text{m})^{-1}\). As printed the quantities are dimensionally not a resistivity and a conductivity at all.]

**Data:** length \( L = 6 \) m, diameter \( d = 0.5 \) mm \( = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \) m, resistance \( R = 50\ \Omega \).

**Step 1 — area of cross section.** The radius is \( r = d/2 = 0.25 \times 10^{-3} \) m, so

\( A = \pi r^{2} = \pi (0.25 \times 10^{-3})^{2} = \pi (6.25 \times 10^{-8}) = 1.9635 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2} \)

**Step 2 — resistivity.** From \( R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} \),

\( \rho = \dfrac{RA}{L} = \dfrac{(50)(1.9635 \times 10^{-7})}{6} = \dfrac{9.8175 \times 10^{-6}}{6} \)

\( \rho = 1.636 \times 10^{-6}\ \Omega\,\text{m} \)

**Step 3 — conductivity.** Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity:

\( \sigma = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \dfrac{1}{1.636 \times 10^{-6}} = 6.112 \times 10^{5}\ (\Omega\,\text{m})^{-1} \)

Note the units carefully: resistivity is measured in \( \Omega\,\text{m} \) (ohm **times** metre, not ohm per metre), and conductivity in \( (\Omega\,\text{m})^{-1} \), equivalently \( \text{S m}^{-1} \) (siemens per metre).

**Answer: \( \rho = 1.64 \times 10^{-6}\ \Omega\,\text{m} \) and \( \sigma = 6.11 \times 10^{5}\ (\Omega\,\text{m})^{-1} \).**

stem:
Find the value of resistances for the following colour code.
1. Blue Green Red Gold
2. Brown Black Red Silver
3. Red Red Orange Gold
4. Orange White Red Gold
5. Yellow Violet Brown Silver
context:
Solve the following problems.

Resistor colour code (from the chapter's table under Fig. 11.7):

| Colour | 1st digit | 2nd digit | Multiplier | Tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Black | 0 | 0 | \( \times 10^{0} \) | |
| Brown | 1 | 1 | \( \times 10^{1} \) | \( \pm 1\% \) |
| Red | 2 | 2 | \( \times 10^{2} \) | \( \pm 2\% \) |
| Orange | 3 | 3 | \( \times 10^{3} \) | |
| Yellow | 4 | 4 | \( \times 10^{4} \) | |
| Green | 5 | 5 | \( \times 10^{5} \) | |
| Blue | 6 | 6 | \( \times 10^{6} \) | |
| Violet | 7 | 7 | \( \times 10^{7} \) | |
| Gray | 8 | 8 | \( \times 10^{8} \) | |
| White | 9 | 9 | \( \times 10^{9} \) | |
| Gold | – | – | \( \times 10^{-1} \) | \( \pm 5\% \) |
| Silver | – | – | \( \times 10^{-2} \) | \( \pm 10\% \) |
| No colour | – | – | – | \( \pm 20\% \) |
our_solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: two of the five printed values are wrong, and one mistake explains both. Item 3, **Red Red Orange Gold**, is \(22 \times 10^{3} = 22\ \text{k}\Omega \pm 5\%\); the key prints \(2.2\ \text{k}\Omega\). Item 5, **Yellow Violet Brown Silver**, is \(47 \times 10^{1} = 470\ \Omega \pm 10\%\); the key prints \(4.70\ \text{k}\Omega\). The three items the key gets right — 1, 2 and 4 — all happen to carry a RED third band, whose multiplier is \(\times 10^{2}\); substituting \(\times 10^{2}\) into items 3 and 5 reproduces the printed answers exactly. The key-setter applied the Red multiplier to all five and ignored the actual third band twice. Read against the chapter's own colour table, Orange is \(\times 10^{3}\) and Brown is \(\times 10^{1}\).]

**Method.** In the four-band code the first two bands give the two significant digits, the third band is the decimal multiplier and the fourth band is the tolerance. Using the table: Black 0, Brown 1, Red 2, Orange 3, Yellow 4, Green 5, Blue 6, Violet 7, Gray 8, White 9; Gold as the fourth band means \( \pm 5\% \) and Silver means \( \pm 10\% \).

\( R = (\text{1st digit} \times 10 + \text{2nd digit}) \times \text{multiplier} \)

**1. Blue Green Red Gold**

Blue \( = 6 \), Green \( = 5 \), Red \( = \times 10^{2} \), Gold \( = \pm 5\% \)

\( R = 65 \times 10^{2} = 6500\ \Omega = 6.5\ \text{k}\Omega \pm 5\% \)

**2. Brown Black Red Silver**

Brown \( = 1 \), Black \( = 0 \), Red \( = \times 10^{2} \), Silver \( = \pm 10\% \)

\( R = 10 \times 10^{2} = 1000\ \Omega = 1\ \text{k}\Omega \pm 10\% \)

**3. Red Red Orange Gold**

Red \( = 2 \), Red \( = 2 \), Orange \( = \times 10^{3} \), Gold \( = \pm 5\% \)

\( R = 22 \times 10^{3} = 22000\ \Omega = 22\ \text{k}\Omega \pm 5\% \)

**4. Orange White Red Gold**

Orange \( = 3 \), White \( = 9 \), Red \( = \times 10^{2} \), Gold \( = \pm 5\% \)

\( R = 39 \times 10^{2} = 3900\ \Omega = 3.9\ \text{k}\Omega \pm 5\% \)

**5. Yellow Violet Brown Silver**

Yellow \( = 4 \), Violet \( = 7 \), Brown \( = \times 10^{1} \), Silver \( = \pm 10\% \)

\( R = 47 \times 10^{1} = 470\ \Omega \pm 10\% \)

**Answers:**

| No. | Colour code | Value | Tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Blue Green Red Gold | \( 6500\ \Omega = 6.5\ \text{k}\Omega \) | \( \pm 5\% \) |
| 2 | Brown Black Red Silver | \( 1000\ \Omega = 1\ \text{k}\Omega \) | \( \pm 10\% \) |
| 3 | Red Red Orange Gold | \( 22000\ \Omega = 22\ \text{k}\Omega \) | \( \pm 5\% \) |
| 4 | Orange White Red Gold | \( 3900\ \Omega = 3.9\ \text{k}\Omega \) | \( \pm 5\% \) |
| 5 | Yellow Violet Brown Silver | \( 470\ \Omega \) | \( \pm 10\% \) |

stem: A current 4A flows through an automobile headlight. How many electrons flow through the headlight in a time 2hrs.
our_solution:
**Data:** current \( I = 4 \) A, time \( t = 2 \) hours, charge on an electron \( e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \) C.

**Step 1 — convert the time to seconds.**

\( t = 2 \times 60 \times 60 = 7200 \) s

**Step 2 — total charge that flows.** Current is charge per unit time, \( I = q/t \), so

\( q = I t = (4)(7200) = 28800 \) C

**Step 3 — number of electrons.** The charge is carried by \( n \) electrons, each of magnitude \( e \), so \( q = n e \) and

\( n = \dfrac{q}{e} = \dfrac{28800}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \)

\( n = 1.8 \times 10^{23} \) electrons

**Answer: \( n = 1.8 \times 10^{23} \) electrons flow through the headlight in 2 hours.**

stem: The heating element connected to 230V draws a current of 5A. Determine the amount of heat dissipated in 1 hour (J = 4.2 J/cal.).
our_solution:
**Data:** \( V = 230 \) V, \( I = 5 \) A, \( t = 1 \) hour \( = 3600 \) s, mechanical equivalent of heat \( J = 4.2 \) J/cal.

**Step 1 — power dissipated.**

\( P = VI = (230)(5) = 1150\ \text{W} \)

**Step 2 — heat produced in one hour (in joules).**

\( W = Pt = VIt = (1150)(3600) \)

\( W = 4.14 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J} \)

**Step 3 — express it in calories.** Since \( 1 \) cal \( = J = 4.2 \) J,

\( H = \dfrac{W}{J} = \dfrac{4.14 \times 10^{6}}{4.2} \)

\( H = 9.857 \times 10^{5}\ \text{cal} \approx 985.7\ \text{kcal} \)

**Answer: the heat dissipated in 1 hour is \( W = 4.14 \times 10^{6} \) J, i.e. \( H = 9.86 \times 10^{5} \) cal (about \( 985.7 \) kcal).**
